name: The Ombu of Piazza Umberto I

location.address: Giardini di Piazza Umberto I, Bari

transport: Bari Centrale railway station, about 5 minutes' walk
story:
Saving one of Bari's four officially monumental trees has been costed at around a thousand euros, and the money has not been spent. The tree is an ombu, it stands in the gardens of Piazza Umberto I five minutes from the central station, and it leans. It leans because it has spent years reaching for light past the holm oaks around it, and because the asphalt laid up to its base has damaged the plate of roots underneath. A local civic association put all of that in a letter to the mayor asking for a modest repair job.

The species is stranger than the tree looks. Phytolacca dioica is not a tree in the botanical sense but an outsized herb from the South American pampas, its trunk swollen with water storing tissue rather than timber, which is why nobody can date one by counting rings. Italy imported it in the middle of the 19th century as an ornamental curiosity, and almost none of those imports ever reached this size. This one is 2.5 metres around and about six metres tall, low and heavy and grey, and both the Puglia and the national registers list it as monumental on those measurements.

Its age is a guess by its own defenders, whose letter says it was probably planted in the 1950s. Nobody has put a firmer date on it. If you know one, tell us.

name: The Mangiafumo of Piazza Umberto I

location.address: Giardini di Piazza Umberto I, Bari

transport: Bari Centrale railway station, about 5 minutes' walk
story:
Bari calls this one la mangiafumo, the smoke-eater, on the local conviction that it swallows the traffic fumes of the streets around it. That part is folklore. What is not folklore is the base: three metres around, swollen into a grey elephantine foot that stores water, sitting in a public garden two minutes from the central station.

Nolina longifolia is a Mexican plant from dry limestone slopes at altitude, and the specimens Europe planted as ornamental curiosities in its gardens almost all stayed modest. This one did not. Three metres of girth under four and a half metres of height was enough for the Puglia and the national registers to list it as a monumental tree, one of only four in the whole of Bari and one of 74 in the region. A second of those four, the ombu, stands a few metres away in the same bed, so a visitor can see half of the city's officially remarkable trees without turning around.

The gardens around it were made by merging two 19th-century ones and rebuilt in 1905 around the equestrian statue of Umberto I. The mangiafumo's own arrival went unrecorded. It lays down no countable rings and no planting date has surfaced, so it comes to this page without even a range. If you know when it went in, tell us.

name: The Pine of Carrassi

location.address: Corso Alcide De Gasperi, corner of Via Ugo La Malfa, Carrassi, Bari

access: Free, public roadside plot. The tree stands in a small enclosed bed behind a low concrete wall right at the street corner, visible and reachable from the pavement at any time; no gate, ticket or permission needed.
transport: Carrassi district, about 3 km south of Bari Centrale station; reachable by city bus along Corso Alcide De Gasperi, no rail nearby.
story:
A branch on this Aleppo pine broke off in a heavy snowfall about two decades ago, and Bari's foresters simply cut the stump flush and left the rest standing, close to six metres round at the trunk. It grows in a fenced bed on a street corner in Carrassi, behind a low concrete wall low enough that generations of neighbourhood kids have climbed over it and up the tree itself, which the local paper reports as an open secret rather than a problem anyone has stopped.

The tree is one of only four in the whole of Bari that Puglia's monumental register recognises, though even the record argues with itself about what it is: the official listing calls it an Aleppo pine, a separate botanical survey calls the same tree a stone pine, and nobody has resolved which. A University of Bari botanist puts its age at roughly a century and a half, the same estimate he gives for a second monumental tree across town, while warning in the same breath that dating either one precisely is close to impossible.

Do not confuse it with the pine that stood one intersection further along the same street and was felled in 2025. This one, at the De Gasperi corner with Via Ugo La Malfa, is still there.
verify_notes: Two independent sources beyond the register: Barinedita (3 Jan 2018, in-person visit) places it exactly at the De Gasperi/Via Ugo La Malfa corner, describes a small plot enclosed by a low concrete wall, trunk split into three main branches, one branch amputated about 20 years before the 2018 article after breaking in heavy snow. Locals use the spot as a landmark (children climb it, couples meet there). Italian Botanical Heritage's English page corroborates location, girth (19 ft = approx 580 cm, matching the register's 570 cm) and rough height, but calls it a 'stone pine (Pinus pinea)' rather than the register's Pinus halepensis (Aleppo pine) - SPECIES CONFLICT, flagged rather than resolved; Barinedita's own text just says 'pino' without a species. Height also disagrees: register says 17 m, both secondary sources converge on about 13 m. Age is an estimate, not a measurement: botanist Pietro Medagli (University of Salento) is quoted giving 'roughly 150 years' for both this pine and the Carbonara leccio (candidate from the same brief, blocked separately for access), while explicitly cautioning that precise dating of either is very difficult; treat 150 as a named expert's best guess, not a derived figure. No sourced confirmation newer than the 2018 article that the tree is still standing, so flagged for that too - but note this is NOT the pine felled in June 2025 (BariToday, 13 June 2025, 'Pino storico in corso Alcide De Gasperi verso l'abbattimento'): that dead tree stood at the De Gasperi corner with Via Pende, a different intersection on the same street, confirmed by the article's own image filename and dateline.
